summary: A user study in which Prolific-recruited programmers used GitHub Copilot CLI (gpt-5.1-codex-max) to assess 148 HIPAA-derived non-functional requirements against the iTrust Java EHR codebase. Each assessment covers satisfaction level, reasoning and code location. Participants agreed with the agent 91–94% of the time, yet accuracy against an expert ground truth was low (satisfaction F1 0.381, code-location F1 0.203). A PARADISE regression links verbosity (negatively) and proactive turns (positively) to user satisfaction.

claims.claim: Participants agree with the agent's NFR assessments 91-94% of the time, but accuracy against expert ground truth is low.
claims.evidence: Fig. 3/Table 5: agreement 91% (satisfaction), 94% (reasoning), 94% (location), means 3.27-3.34 on 1-4 scale; Table 4: satisfaction-level F1 0.381 (vs 0.25 chance), reasoning BERTScore F1 0.520, code-location F1 0.203. Ground truth built by one expert and reviewed by a second (no independent double-annotation or kappa for ground truth).

claims.claim: Reported code-location metrics are internally consistent.
claims.evidence: Table 4 gives code-location precision 0.151 and recall 0.142 but F1 0.203; if F1 is averaged per item it cannot exceed the mean of P and R (0.1465), so the averaging scheme or subset differs and is not explained.

claims.claim: Verbose responses and many information-providing turns lower satisfaction; proactive interaction raises it.
claims.evidence: Table 7: standardized β = -0.583 (p=.002), -0.485 (p=.006), +0.422 (p=.015) from backward elimination over 21 predictors on 32 dialogues after outlier removal — high risk of overfitting, which the authors acknowledge in §7.

claims.claim: 49 programmers were hired to interact with Copilot.
claims.evidence: §3.4: 8 pilot + 41 main participants; 15 removed after screening, leaving 34 dialogues (Table 3), and 32 for regression. The abstract's 49 includes pilot and excluded participants.

patterns.note: Human reviewers rubber-stamp convincing but wrong agent assessments (91%+ agreement vs F1 0.381), so a human approval gate alone is weak for compliance NFRs.
Structured NFRs with explicit satisfaction levels/locations make agent errors measurable, but the agent cannot reliably assess them.
Relevant to spec-driven traceability (requirement -> code location); agent-generated trace links have F1 ~0.2.
Code localization for cross-cutting requirements is poor; no retrieval tooling compared.

methodology.sample: 148 NFRs; 34 usable dialogues (406 turns) from Prolific participants; each NFR assigned to ≥2 participants; 32 dialogues in regression.
methodology.baselines: Chance (0.25) for satisfaction level only; no other agent/model or non-AI condition.
methodology.models: Single: GitHub Copilot CLI with gpt-5.1-codex-max.
methodology.variance: One-sample t-tests on agreement; regression SEs reported; no repeated agent runs.
methodology.contamination_controls: None; iTrust is a public academic codebase likely in pretraining.

biases.detail: One agent/model on one codebase in one regulatory domain (acknowledged).
34 dialogues; 21-predictor backward elimination on 32 data points.
Prolific crowd-workers without HIPAA expertise judge compliance; agreement may reflect lack of expertise rather than over-trust (acknowledged).
Lexical/embedding metrics (ROUGE, BERTScore) for reasoning quality; code-location F1 inconsistent with P/R.
Ground truth by one expert with second-expert review rather than independent double coding.

coi.affiliations: University of Maine; University of Notre Dame.
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: GitHub Copilot / OpenAI gpt-5.1-codex-max, evaluated unfavorably.
coi.detail: Academic, public funding; no vendor ties.

verdict_reason: Peer-reviewed, IRB-approved, data released, and it targets a healthcare-compliance Java codebase, but it uses a single model, few usable dialogues, a fragile regression, and a code-location metric inconsistency.
applicability: Directly relevant warning for a healthcare-education Java team adopting spec-driven development. Do not let an agent's self-assessment of whether NFRs (privacy, HIPAA/FERPA-like handling of learner or patient data) are satisfied, plus a quick human 'looks right', count as verification: reviewers agreed 91%+ with assessments that were mostly wrong. Express compliance NFRs as executable checks (tests, static rules, data-flow scans) in each of the ≥4 ingestion repos. Require agents to cite exact file:line evidence that a deterministic tool re-checks. Keep agent responses short and proactive. The results come from one model and one codebase, so re-measure on your own stack.
